probing_questions: What does the text claim must be the case, and what kind of necessity is invoked?
What does the text claim could be different, and how is this possibility established?
What object, quantifier, condition and time fall under each modal operator?
Does a necessary exposure or capacity leave actual realization contingent?
Does the text distinguish between different grades of necessity and possibility?
What conceptual, empirical, normative or practical warrant supports this exact force?
Are modal operators used consistently, or do they shift meaning across contexts?
Does an alleged change concern the same proposition and conditions, or a distinct claim?
What background assumptions does the scenario take for granted?
Does conceivability in the thought experiment genuinely establish possibility?
Which alternative does the text itself consider, and does it vary the condition relevant to this claim?
Where does the text assert a sharp boundary between categories?
Does the text acknowledge vagueness and gradual transitions, or does it impose false precision?

key_concepts.definition: Modality concerning what reality allows — what is metaphysically possible, necessary, or contingent. A claim is alethically necessary if it holds in all possible worlds (or all worlds with the same fundamental laws), possible if it holds in at least one, contingent if it holds in some but not all. This is the deepest modal layer, concerning the very structure of reality rather than our knowledge or obligations.
key_concepts.name: alethic_modality

key_concepts.definition: Modality concerning what is consistent with what we know — what we can rule out, what remains open. 'The culprit might be the butler' expresses epistemic possibility (we cannot eliminate this hypothesis), not metaphysical possibility. Confusing epistemic with alethic modality is a pervasive error: 'we cannot rule it out' does not entail 'it could actually happen.'
key_concepts.name: epistemic_modality

key_concepts.definition: Modality concerning obligation and permission — what ought to be, what may be, what must not be. Deontic necessity (obligation) is structurally analogous to alethic necessity but operates in the normative rather than descriptive domain. The is-ought gap means deontic claims require distinct justification from alethic claims; deriving 'must' (deontic) from 'is' (alethic) is a classic fallacy.
key_concepts.name: deontic_modality

key_concepts.definition: Complete consistent descriptions of how reality could be. A possible world specifies a truth value for every proposition in a way that respects logical constraints. Modal claims are analyzed as claims about which possible worlds satisfy them: necessity means all worlds, possibility means at least one. Whether possible worlds are abstract representations or concrete realities is contested, but the framework is indispensable for rigorous modal analysis.
key_concepts.name: possible_worlds

key_concepts.definition: Different strengths and sources of necessity: logical necessity (following from the laws of logic alone), metaphysical necessity (following from the nature of things), physical necessity (following from natural laws), and practical necessity (following from circumstances and constraints). Conflating these types — treating practical necessity as if it were logical necessity — is a common source of modal overreach.
key_concepts.name: necessity_types

key_concepts.definition: Vulnerability to the sorites (heap) paradox: if removing one grain from a heap still leaves a heap, then by repeated application no grains yield a heap. Arguments drawing sharp boundaries on continuous dimensions are sorites-susceptible. Claims that 'at point X, A becomes B' (reform becomes revolution, collection becomes heap) often mask arbitrary boundary-drawing with the appearance of necessity.
key_concepts.name: sorites_susceptibility

key_concepts.definition: The property of a conclusion that it survives across reasonable variations in the thought experiment's setup. A robust modal conclusion holds not just in the specific imagined scenario but across a range of similar scenarios. Lack of robustness suggests the conclusion depends on arbitrary features of the example rather than establishing genuine necessity or possibility.
key_concepts.name: counterfactual_robustness

key_concepts.definition: An error in reasoning involving modal operators. Common forms include: scope fallacy (confusing 'necessarily, if P then Q' with 'if P then necessarily Q'), type confusion (treating epistemic possibility as metaphysical possibility), probabilistic confusion (treating possibility as likelihood), and necessity inflation (claiming logical necessity where only practical necessity holds).
key_concepts.name: modal_fallacy

primary.description: Saul Kripke (1940–2022), American philosopher and logician whose development of possible worlds semantics revolutionized modal logic and provided the formal apparatus for analyzing necessity, possibility, and contingency. His 1963 paper on semantical considerations established the accessibility relation between possible worlds, allowing precise characterization of different modal systems. His 1972 lectures 'Naming and Necessity' distinguished between epistemic and metaphysical necessity, showing that some truths are necessary but only knowable a posteriori (necessary a posteriori) while others are contingent but knowable a priori. This distinction is foundational for this engine's capacity to separate different types of modal claims and evaluate their distinct justification requirements.
primary.name: kripke

secondary.description: David Lewis (1941–2001), American philosopher whose modal realism treated possible worlds as concrete entities rather than abstract constructs. His 1986 work 'On the Plurality of Worlds' provided the most systematic defense of taking modal talk literally, treating 'possibly P' as 'there exists a world where P.' Even for those who reject his ontology, Lewis's framework clarifies counterfactual reasoning, establishes criteria for world-similarity, and provides tools for evaluating thought experiments. His analysis of counterfactual conditionals grounds this engine's approach to branching possibility structures.
secondary.name: lewis

secondary.description: Timothy Williamson (1955–), British philosopher whose work on modal epistemology addresses how we can know modal truths. His 2007 'The Philosophy of Philosophy' argues that modal knowledge derives from our capacity for counterfactual reasoning rather than from special rational intuition. This grounds the engine's attention to how modal claims are justified and whether purported modal knowledge rests on legitimate counterfactual imagination or mere failure of imagination.
secondary.name: williamson

secondary.description: Angelika Kratzer (1945–), German-American linguist whose formal semantics for modality in natural language distinguishes between different modal bases (epistemic, deontic, circumstantial) and ordering sources. Her framework explains why 'must' in 'You must be the new neighbor' (epistemic) differs from 'must' in 'You must pay your taxes' (deontic). This informs the engine's classification of modal claims by modality type.
secondary.name: kratzer

secondary.description: Aristotle (384–322 BCE), whose modal syllogistic in the 'Prior Analytics' was the first systematic treatment of modal reasoning. His distinction between what is actual, what is possible, and what is necessary established the foundational categories that persist in contemporary modal logic. His concept of potentiality (dunamis) versus actuality (energeia) provides philosophical grounding for understanding how possibilities relate to actualization.
secondary.name: aristotle

traditions.description: The formal tradition treating modal operators as quantifiers over possible worlds. Necessity becomes universal quantification (true in all accessible worlds), possibility becomes existential quantification (true in some accessible world). Different accessibility relations yield different modal logics. This provides the formal backbone for analyzing modal claims with precision and detecting when modal operators are used inconsistently.
traditions.name: possible_worlds_semantics

traditions.description: The philosophical tradition investigating the nature of modality itself — whether modal facts are primitive or reducible, whether possible worlds are abstract or concrete, how modal truths are grounded. Debates between actualists (only the actual world exists) and possibilists (possible worlds exist too) shape how we understand what modal claims are about. This tradition informs the engine's sensitivity to different philosophical frameworks underlying modal reasoning.
traditions.name: analytic_modal_metaphysics

traditions.description: The philosophical practice of using imagined scenarios to test principles, identify necessary conditions, or establish possibility. From Galileo's ship to Rawls's veil of ignorance, thought experiments are central to philosophical argument. Critical analysis of this methodology — what makes a thought experiment probative, what assumptions it smuggles in, how robust its conclusions are — is essential for evaluating modal claims based on conceivability.
traditions.name: thought_experiment_methodology

traditions.description: The formal study of obligation, permission, and prohibition as modal operators. Just as necessity and possibility govern what must be and what can be, obligation and permission govern what ought to be and what may be. The analogies and disanalogies between alethic and deontic modality — including the notorious is-ought gap — are central to evaluating arguments that move between descriptive and normative modal claims.
traditions.name: deontic_logic

traditions.description: The formal study of knowledge and belief as modal operators, where 'knowing that P' implies that P is true in all worlds compatible with what the agent knows. This tradition distinguishes between what is epistemically possible (consistent with our knowledge) and what is metaphysically possible (consistent with reality). The conflation of these is a common modal fallacy that this engine is designed to detect.
traditions.name: epistemic_logic

traditions.description: The study of conditionals concerning what would have happened if things had been different. Lewis's similarity-based semantics, where counterfactuals are evaluated by looking at the most similar worlds where the antecedent holds, provides tools for assessing branching possibility structures. This tradition grounds the engine's analysis of alternative scenarios and their probability assignments.
traditions.name: counterfactual_reasoning

problematique: An operator inventory a reader can inspect: exact proposition and owner, must/may/cannot/ought or epistemic hedge, type and scope, supporting warrant, justified force and available alternative. Lead with the most consequential force distinction. Desks lift modal-claim and force-change tables; useful coverage is the product, with no compulsory discovery of equivocation. Text containing modal claims or thought experiments; extra evidence only when the claim invokes it.
researcher_question: What does the text claim must, may or cannot hold, and what supports that force?
